Describing the data

The aim of the following code is to broadly describe the data before diving into a more specific analysis.

Loading libraries and the data

library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

load(here("data", "03_cancer_augment.RData"))

Exploring the patients

clinical_augment |> 
  group_by(sex, status) |> 
  count() |>
  group_by(sex) |> 
  mutate(percentage = (n/sum(n))*100)
# A tibble: 4 × 4
# Groups:   sex [2]
  sex    status       n percentage
  <chr>  <chr>    <int>      <dbl>
1 Female DECEASED   314       51.7
2 Female LIVING     293       48.3
3 Male   DECEASED   488       48.7
4 Male   LIVING     515       51.3

The patients in this study are about two thirds men to one third women, with roughly a 50% survival rate, though survival of women is slightly lower than that of men on first inspection.

Status and gender

Visualizing the LIVING and DECEASED patients based on gender and age group.

p1 <- clinical_augment |> 
        ggplot(aes(x = sex,
                   fill = status))+
        geom_bar(alpha = 0.5)+
  labs(x= "",
       y = "Number of patients",
       fill = "Status",
       title = "Profiles of the patients in the cancer study")+
  theme_minimal()
p2 <- ggplot(data = clinical_augment,
       mapping = aes(x = status,
                     y = sex,
                     colour = age_group))+
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10)+
  geom_count(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
             alpha = 0.5)+
  labs(size = "Count",
       x = "Status",
       y = "",
       colour = "Age")+
  theme_minimal()

p1+p2+ plot_layout(widths = c(1, 5))

Few patients are under 30 years old, with most in the 61-70 age group. WHAT CAN BE SAID ABOUT THE POSITION OF THE DOTS ON THE GRID ?

clinical_augment |> 
  group_by(cancer_type, sex) |> 
  count() |>
  group_by(cancer_type) |> 
  mutate(affects_both_sex = if_else(n()>1,
                                    TRUE,
                                    FALSE))
# A tibble: 20 × 4
# Groups:   cancer_type [11]
   cancer_type                sex        n affects_both_sex
   <chr>                      <chr>  <int> <lgl>           
 1 Bladder Cancer             Female    51 TRUE            
 2 Bladder Cancer             Male     160 TRUE            
 3 Breast Cancer              Female    41 FALSE           
 4 Cancer of Unknown Primary  Female    42 TRUE            
 5 Cancer of Unknown Primary  Male      43 TRUE            
 6 Colorectal Cancer          Female    48 TRUE            
 7 Colorectal Cancer          Male      61 TRUE

 9 Esophagogastric Cancer     Male      91 TRUE            
10 Glioma                     Female    39 TRUE            
11 Glioma                     Male      77 TRUE            
12 Head and Neck Cancer       Female    27 TRUE            
13 Head and Neck Cancer       Male     102 TRUE            
14 Melanoma                   Female   115 TRUE            
15 Melanoma                   Male     198 TRUE            
16 Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Female   178 TRUE            
17 Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Male     166 TRUE            
18 Renal Cell Carcinoma       Female    39 TRUE            
19 Renal Cell Carcinoma       Male     104 TRUE            
20 Skin Cancer, Non-Melanoma  Male       1 FALSE

Eleven types of cancer are tracked in this data set, two of which (breast cancer and skin cancer) affect only women or men respectively. Only one patient was affected by skin cancer.

clinical_augment |> 
  filter(status == "DECEASED") |> 
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(average_survival_months = mean(os_months)) |> 
  arrange(average_survival_months)
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  age_group average_survival_months
  <fct>                       <dbl>
1 <30                          7.28
2 >71                          8.95
3 61-70                        8.98
4 31-50                        9.35
5 50-60                       10.7

The variation in survival of the deceased patients is similar among age groups, though the patients under 30 years old have the lowest, while the patients between 50 and 60 have the highest.

Exploring the types of mutations

Visualizing the number of mutations that affect each patient.

ggplot(data = clinical_augment,
       mapping = aes(x = cancer_type,
                     y = total_mutations,
                     color = cancer_type)) +
  geom_jitter() +
    theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(title = "Cancer type and number of mutations", 
       subtitle = "The dots indicate how many mutations the individual patient has",
       x = "Cancer type",
       y = "Number of mutations") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

EXPLANATION

clinical_mutation |> 
  filter(is_top_gene) |> 
  group_by(hugo_symbol) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = hugo_symbol,
             fill = cancer_type))+
  geom_bar(alpha = 0.5)+
  labs(title = "Number of mutations associated to top 20 genes",
       x = "Hugo symbol of affected gene",
       y = "Number of mutations",
       fill = "Cancer type")+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
    angle = 45,
    hjust = 1))

There are big variations in the number of genes with mutations. The TP53 gene is the most mutated gene in this data set and appears in all the cancer types.

mutation_augment |> 
  group_by(hugo_symbol) |> 
  count(name = "nbr_occurences") |>
  ungroup() |> 
  summarise(mean = mean(nbr_occurences),
            max = max(nbr_occurences),
            min = min(nbr_occurences),
            median = median(nbr_occurences))
# A tibble: 1 × 4
   mean   max   min median
  <dbl> <int> <int>  <dbl>
1  43.5   834     1   22.5

This table summarizes the number of mutations affecting each gene. This shows the considerable variation in how genes are affected in all types of cancer.
